gao-gaoreports-gao-00-5337r:
Noncitizens held for crimes in U.S. prisons and jails are the subject of GAO-00-5337R, a letter report sent to House members on April 7, 2005. The federal government pays the full cost in federal prisons. It pays part of the cost in state prisons and local jails through the State Criminal Alien Assistance Program.

GAO counted about 49,000 such inmates in federal prisons at the end of 2004, about 27 percent of all federal inmates. Total federal costs for 2001 through 2004 came to about $5.8 billion. Aid to states and local jails covered a quarter or less of their costs. Counts, costs, and aid gaps fill the text.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-247r:
Management Report, GAO-05-247R of April 27, 2005, lists soft spots in the tax agency's inner checks that its main audit left aside. In November 2004, GAO gave its audit of the Internal Revenue Service's books for fiscal years 2004 and 2003. That audit judged the books, the checks, and the tie to the law. This side report holds the rest.

The faults here drew no open advice yet, but each merits a chief's eye, GAO says. They span cash systems, staff vetting, backup plans, and tax liens, per the index terms. A mate report on the fate of past advice was set to follow soon after.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-27r:
Applying Agreed-Upon Procedures: Federal Unemployment Taxes, GAO-05-27R of November 5, 2005, holds a set of checks run for GAO on jobless tax cash. The test asks if the net federal unemployment tax sent to the Unemployment Trust Fund for the fiscal year ended September 30, 2004, rests on sound records. The work ran under U.S. audit rules for such set tasks.

The checks test the deals that form the sums sent to the fund. They match tax agency records to Treasury records at key points. The text states plainly what such a task can and cannot vow. GAO owns the call on whether the steps were fit for its aim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-337r:
A report-form twin of a letter sent the same day, GAO-05-337R of April 7, 2005, answers three set queries on noncitizens held for crimes in U.S. lockups. Congress posed the queries for three tiers of custody: federal prisons, state prisons, and local jails. For aid-paid cases, the cash path runs through the State Criminal Alien Assistance Program at the Justice Department.

Query one asks how many such inmates each tier held in the past few years. Query two asks their lands of birth or citizenship. Query three asks what their keep cost at each tier. State and local chiefs say aid pays too small a share; the data let readers weigh that claim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-387r:
Veterans Health Care, GAO-05-387R of March 23, 2005, is a letter that maps the aid role of veterans' halls in a national crunch. Since the attacks of September 11, 2001, the agency has honed its plans for terror and storm. In August 2004, law arms warned that VA and military halls could be marks. War hurt from Iraq and Afghanistan fill the halls at the same time.

Congress asked three things. It asked what aid the halls owe troops in war and in a crunch at home. It asked what the agency does to keep its own work in flow. It asked how the halls team with peers at each tier.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-467r:
Computer security at the Bureau of the Public Debt is the subject of a GAO letter, GAO-05-467R, sent on April 18, 2005. The letter grew out of GAO's audit of the federal debt schedules for fiscal years 2003 and 2004. GAO tested the general and program-level security controls over the bureau's key financial systems. It also followed up on fixes promised after audits in earlier years.

Overall controls were judged effective in all material respects. Even so, testing found six new issues, all tied to access controls. GAO made six recommendations in a separate limited-use report. Of seven older recommendations, four had been fully carried out by September 30, 2004. Work on the other three was still under way. The bureau later told GAO that seven of the eight open issues were fully resolved. The letter gives a short audit record of where debt systems stood.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-507r:
Italian American War Veterans of the United States is the corporation behind GAO letter GAO-05-507R, sent on June 10, 2005. The group keeps alive the memory and records of patriotic service by Italian American men and women in the Armed Forces. The audit report reviewed here covers its fiscal year ended August 31, 2003.

The pattern of review matches the charter statute. Yearly statements must give assets, liabilities, income, and expenses in fair detail. An independent public accountant must audit them. GAO read the statements, the notes, and the auditor's report, and checked the numbers in a limited way. It also discussed possible reporting upgrades with the auditor. GAO found no noncompliance worth reporting to the House Judiciary Committee. One point sets this letter apart: the auditor judged the statements fairly presented on a modified cash basis of accounting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-587r:
The Defense Department's management representation letter for fiscal year 2004 is faulted in GAO report GAO-05-587R, dated June 23, 2005. Such letters back the audit of the government's consolidated financial statements. Agency leaders confirm in writing what they told auditors about their books. GAO checked the department's letter against five key conditions drawn from the federal audit manual.

Faults showed in three of the five areas. The letter was not signed at the right level of management. It gave no materiality thresholds, the cut-off points that show which matters count as big. Treasury and the budget office need those agency cut-offs to set their own. The letter held 22 of the 28 standard representations that applied. Four more were partial, and 2 were missing in full. GAO made three recommendations to the department's chief financial officer. It also asked the inspector general to help ensure that future letters meet the standard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-597r:
GAO letter GAO-05-597R, sent on July 14, 2005, reviews the Energy Department's management representation letter for fiscal year 2004. The letter is part of the evidence base for the audit of the government's consolidated statements. GAO examined five key areas and found two that needed work. Neither fault went to the letter's main confirmations, which were nearly complete.

The letter held 28 of the 29 standard representations that applied to the department. The last one was present only in part. The other fault sat in the error reporting. The department gave a summary of uncorrected misstatements, but it did not split them by kind. Errors in accounts with other agencies were not separated from errors in accounts with the public. GAO made two recommendations to the chief financial officer. It asked the inspector general, with the outside audit firm, to help police future letters. Both offices agreed with the recommendations.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-607r:
The Export-Import Bank's fiscal year 2004 letter drew its own review, GAO report GAO-05-607R of July 22, 2005. GAO judged the letter against five key areas and found one needing work. The bank included 24 of the 26 standard representations that applied to it.

One of the other two was only partly stated, and one was missing in full. GAO told the bank's Chief Financial Officer to include every applicable representation in later letters. It asked the audit committee director, with the outside audit firm, to help. The finance chief said the bank would add the required wording in its fiscal 2005 letter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-647r:
Planned specialty hospitals are counted in GAO-05-647R, a letter of May 19, 2005. A 2003 law paused new physician-owned hospitals focused on one field, but let projects already under way seek exemption. The Medicare agency got 40 such pleas: 38 new hospitals and 2 expansions. Surgical hospitals led with 22, then cardiac with 9. Texas filed 19 pleas alone. Twelve won approval, two were denied, and one was withdrawn by May.

Beyond the pause, trade groups pointed to 52 more planned sites. GAO could confirm only 6 as physician-owned specialty projects. Growth looks set to resume when the pause ends.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-697r:
A debt swap between Washington and the states sits unused, GAO letter GAO-05-697R reports on July 26, 2005. A 1996 law lets each side skim the other's payments to collect unpaid debts, once they sign a reciprocal pact. No state has signed for contractor payments, and the Treasury's payment arm never pushed the idea. Officials in 17 states GAO called had never heard of the provision. All liked it once told.

In fiscal 2004 the payment arm sent about $1.8 billion to over 4,600 federal contractors who owed some $17 million in state taxes. States could have taken over half of that debt.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-837r:
Converter box subsidies for digital TV are costed in GAO-05-837R, a letter dated June 20, 2005. Congress weighed a rebate for low-income homes that rely on over-the-air signals. Lawmakers listed the admin steps such a program might need. They asked GAO to price those steps. The letter answers that request.

GAO warned that firm prices are hard to give. What the steps would require is deeply uncertain. Past rebate and voucher programs GAO reviewed spent 10 percent to 39 percent on administration. But those programs differ in scope from a TV subsidy. So their costs may not transfer well, GAO said. The letter gives Congress the ranges and the caveats side by side.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1067r:
Posthearing questions on improper payments fill GAO-06-1067R, a letter dated September 6, 2006. GAO had testified on March 9, 2006, at a hearing styled as a report card on agency progress. The testimony covered agency struggles with a 2002 payments law. It rested on fiscal year 2005 agency reports. Lawmakers sent follow-up questions after the hearing.

The questions probe weak spots by agency. One asks about the Homeland Security department's failure to comply, and its wider financial management. Another asks which agencies claiming no at-risk programs draw GAO concern. Social Security overpayment reporting and the aid agency's reporting also get questions. The letter answers them for the record. It sharpens the hearing's verdicts into agency-specific findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1077r:
The long-term fiscal outlook is updated in GAO-06-1077R, a letter dated September 15, 2006. Since 1992, GAO has run simulations of deficits and debt under varied policy paths. It updates them three times a year as new estimates land. The model answers a bipartisan request from members worried about long-term policy effects. This is the September 2006 update.

The letter repeats GAO's 1992 warning, which it calls as relevant today. The federal budget is structurally unbalanced, the warning runs. That will do growing damage and cannot last. Prompt, meaningful action is essential, and delay makes the cure more painful. The update refreshes the numbers behind that verdict with the latest budget outlook and trustee reports. Readers get the long view in compact form.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-127r:
Childhood obesity and what experts say works against it are covered in GAO-06-127R, a letter report dated October 7, 2005. In 30 years the share of obese children has climbed across the United States. Rates more than tripled for children ages 6 to 11. About 9 million children over age 6 were classed as obese. Obese children face more high blood pressure and type II diabetes. Hospital costs tied to childhood obesity more than tripled between 1979 and 1999, reaching $127 million.

GAO asked experts what marks a successful program for children. Most experts pointed to physical activity as a key element. They also stressed the use of best practices drawn from tested programs. The letter gathers that expert judgment for lawmakers who fund prevention work. It frames obesity as a long-term health cost, not just a childhood concern.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-147r:
Global malaria control and the money behind it are surveyed in GAO-06-147R, a letter report dated November 16, 2005. Malaria sickens hundreds of millions of people each year and kills over 1 million. Over 80 percent of deaths occur in Africa, mostly among children under age 5. Simple, cheap methods can prevent and treat the disease. The United States aids endemic nations through its aid agency. It also gives through the Global Fund and the Roll Back Malaria Partnership.

Congress asked GAO to map U.S. investments in national malaria programs. It also asked about the chief hurdles those programs face and how to beat them. Programs must reach remote areas, fund steady supplies of drugs and nets, and track results. Weak health systems in endemic nations strain each step. The letter weighs whether current efforts are as strong as they could be.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-157r:
A small feed testing program for mad cow disease is evaluated in GAO-06-157R, a letter report dated October 11, 2005. Since 1997 federal rules have barred most mammal protein from cattle feed. That feed ban is the main shield against bovine spongiform encephalopathy. The disease spreads through feed laced with tainted tissue. In 2003 the Food and Drug Administration began a small program to test feed directly. GAO had twice reviewed the agency's wider feed ban work, in 2002 and in February 2005.

Those reviews found real steps forward, plus room to improve. This letter judges the testing program itself as an oversight tool. GAO weighed how the tests were chosen, run, and used. It made recommendations to make the program a sharper check on feed makers. The letter adds a narrow but pointed piece to the record on guarding the cattle herd.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-17r:
Medicare payment rates for certain hospital outpatient drugs are critiqued in GAO-06-17R, a letter report dated October 31, 2005. The 2003 Medicare law set a class of drugs paid one by one, not in service bundles. For 2006, rates for these drugs must equal hospitals' average purchase costs. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services proposed rates in July 2005. The law had already sent GAO to survey what hospitals truly pay. GAO sent its survey results to the health secretary for use in rate setting.

GAO urged the secretary to rethink the proposed rates for the drug class. Rebates shape true purchase costs, and the rates should track average price more closely. For radiopharmaceuticals, GAO faulted a plan to rest rates only on cost estimates. Real price data for key products were at hand.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-197r:
Federal unemployment tax flows are checked in GAO-06-197R, a letter report dated November 4, 2005. GAO helped the Department of Labor test one claim: that the net federal unemployment tax revenue sent to the Unemployment Trust Fund rests on sound records. The work covers the fiscal year that ended September 30, 2005. GAO ran a set of agreed-upon procedures with the department. Such work tests set items rather than giving a full audit opinion.

The procedures traced the deals that make up the sums sent to the fund. They also matched Internal Revenue Service records against Treasury records in key reconciliations. GAO worked under government auditing standards, which include the attestation rules of the accounting profession. Those rules also guide how such checks are run and reported. The letter gives the Labor Department a verified base for the year's trust fund figures.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-217r:
Chemical safety laws in three places are compared in GAO-06-217R, a letter report dated November 4, 2005. Chemicals fill daily life, from cleaners and paints to fuels and plastics. Some, like lead and mercury, can badly harm health and nature. The 1976 Toxic Substances Control Act lets the Environmental Protection Agency police chemicals that pose an undue risk. It covers new chemicals before sale and old ones already in trade. Some classes, such as pesticides and drugs, sit under other laws.

Congress asked GAO to set the U.S. law beside its peers. The peers are Canada's protection act and the European Union's current rules. A proposed European overhaul, known as REACH, joins the comparison. The letter lays out how each system tests, reviews, and limits chemicals. It gives lawmakers a side-by-side view as they weigh reform at home. No single model wins on every point.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-37r:
A veterans' club with a federal charter still must show clean books. Letter GAO-06-37R, dated October 7, 2005, reviews the audit of the Navy Club of the United States of America. The audit covers the fiscal year ended July 31, 2003. The club promotes the Navy, Marines, and Coast Guard. It also honors service members who have died.

Under 36 U.S.C. 10101, such corporations must file annual financial statements. They must also get an audit by an independent public accountant. GAO read the statements and the auditor's report. It found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly under U.S. accounting rules.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-457r:
A children's health program faced a subtle risk: states might claim a higher match for the wrong children. Letter GAO-06-457R, dated March 9, 2006, reviews inspector general studies of the State Children's Health Insurance Program. Congress created the program in 1997 for children in families earning too much for Medicaid. It set aside $40 billion over 10 years. States may expand Medicaid, run a separate program, or combine both.

GAO judged work by the Health and Human Services inspector general. The studies counted Medicaid-eligible children placed in separate programs. They also tracked progress in cutting the number of uninsured children. Readers get a check on another watchdog's work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-507r:
Flight pioneers are honored by a hall of fame with a federal charter. Letter GAO-06-507R, dated March 14, 2006, reviews the Aviation Hall of Fame audit. The reports cover fiscal years 2003 and 2002. The hall's purpose is to preserve and memorialize the work of people who advanced aviation in the United States. That mission shapes the corporation behind the statements.

GAO read the financial statements and the auditor's reports. It checked for failures to meet the law's reporting rules. GAO found no reportable instance of noncompliance. The auditor said the statements were presented fairly. They followed generally accepted accounting principles. Readers get a brief, clean audit review.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-687r:
A tropical garden's books get a federal check in GAO-06-687R, a letter report GAO issued on May 12, 2006. The National Tropical Botanical Garden is a federally chartered corporation. It works to encourage and conduct research in basic and applied tropical botany. Like other chartered groups, it must file annual financial statements and have them audited by an outside accountant. GAO reviewed those audits for fiscal years 2003 and 2002.

GAO read the statements and the reports that came with them. GAO found no reportable instances of noncompliance with the financial reporting requirements of the law. The auditor's opinion said the statements were presented fairly under United States accounting principles. GAO's brief letter records the result for Congress. It completes the charter review cycle for those two years.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-717r:
A cancelled jet engine program is the subject of GAO-06-717R, a letter report dated May 22, 2006. The Defense Department planned to buy about 2,400 Joint Strike Fighter aircraft. Foreign sales could add 2,000 to 3,500 more planes. Two engine makers had competed to power the jet, until the department cancelled the alternate engine program. GAO reviewed the analysis behind that choice.

GAO concluded that the cancellation was not based on a comprehensive analysis. The department had not fully weighed the long-term costs of ending competition. Lifetime engine support and spare parts made the stakes very large. The department disputed parts of GAO's reading in its comments. GAO stood by its view that a fuller analysis was needed before such a costly call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-767r:
Bus safety rules for preschoolers are tracked in GAO-06-767R, a letter report dated July 27, 2006. Motor vehicle crashes are the leading cause of death for children ages 3 to 7. Head Start, the federal early learning program for low-income children, serves about 900,000 children. Many local programs bus children to and from centers, though transport is not required. New federal rules set safety duties for that transport, covering buses, restraints, and driver training.

GAO reported on progress and challenges as local programs put the rules in place. Programs faced costs for new buses and child restraints, and deadlines that strained small budgets. Training and record duties also took time to build. The letter gives Congress a ground-level sense of how a safety rule lands in a grant program.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-77r:
River contamination near a nuclear site is the subject of GAO-06-77R, a letter report dated November 4, 2005. The Energy Department's Hanford site in southeastern Washington was built in 1943 to make plutonium for defense. It covers 586 square miles near Richland, Pasco, and Kennewick, home to over 200,000 people. The Columbia River, the nation's second largest, flows past the site. GAO shared early facts on whether site contamination could reach the river.

GAO explained how buried waste has seeped into the soil and rock above the groundwater. These contaminant plumes spread downward and outward from their sources. When a plume reaches groundwater, the pollution can move toward the river. The letter stresses that its information is preliminary. It frames the pathways that later cleanup decisions must address.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-817r:
NASA's return to deep space exploration is questioned in GAO-06-817R, a letter report dated July 17, 2006. NASA plans to spend nearly $230 billion over the next two decades on the Vision for Space Exploration. In January 2006, it released its Exploration Systems Architecture Study, which set the best path to carry out the plan. GAO reviewed that architecture and the strategy for building the new Crew Exploration Vehicle.

GAO's title states its core point: long-term commitment requires more knowledge. GAO probed whether the chosen design fits within projected budgets. It also weighed the risks in NASA's acquisition strategy for the crew vehicle. Past GAO work warns against committing billions before designs are proven. The letter urges NASA to ground its boldest plan in firmer cost and technical facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-837r:
Military survivor benefits and their funding soundness are reviewed in GAO-06-837R, a letter report dated July 26, 2006. The Survivor Benefit Plan pays income to the dependents of service members who die. It sits inside the Military Retirement Fund. Congress changed the plan's coverage and benefits several times in recent years. Lawmakers required GAO to report on what those changes do to the plan's actuarial soundness.

GAO found that the major statutory changes of the past seven fiscal years raised costs. Both defense normal cost payments and Treasury amortization payments to the fund grew. Those higher payments keep the fund sound as benefits expand. When coverage changes, defense actuaries compute the needed contributions. The letter shows the price tag that follows each benefit improvement.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-87r:
Health benefit costs in public-private job contests form the core of GAO letter GAO-06-87R, dated November 17, 2005. Office of Management and Budget Circular A-76 sets how agencies weigh in-house staff against private firms for a task. The aim is a fair contest, with full in-house costs counted.

GAO wrote while reviewing how health benefit costs show up in Defense Department contests. It flagged a gap: the Circular lacked a clear health benefit cost factor. That gap could skew the cost match between public and private bids. The letter gives Congress and agency staff a short, focused warning on one costing flaw.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-907r:
Pay and perks for top staff at nonprofit hospital systems are surveyed in GAO letter GAO-06-907R, dated June 30, 2006. Congress, in its watch over the nonprofit sector, asked how selected systems set salaries, benefits, travel, gifts, and fun spending for their executives.

GAO asked what board structures guard executive pay at the systems studied. It asked what pay and benefits rested on, and what controls covered travel, gifts, and perks. The letter sends Congress the June 5, 2006 staff briefing, with added notes. It gives lawmakers a fact base on nonprofit pay practice, without rating any one system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-927r:
A memorial group for Jewish war veterans is the subject of GAO letter GAO-06-927R, dated July 7, 2006. The Jewish War Veterans, U.S.A., National Memorial keeps a memorial and museum for Americans of the Jewish faith who served in U.S. forces. Its federal charter sets a yearly audit duty.

GAO read the audit reports for fiscal years 2005 and 2004, years that ended March 31. The auditors held the statements fairly shown under U.S. accounting rules. GAO found no breach that had to be reported. The brief letter files that clean result with Congress, in line with the charter audit rules in title 36.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-947r:
A stalled data project at the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-06-947R, dated July 14, 2006. The network, known as FinCEN, fights money laundering. Since 1990 it has run data filed under the Bank Secrecy Act.

Its BSA Direct project aimed to give web tools for that data. By spring 2006 the retrieval and sharing part was set to miss its June 30, 2006 launch date. Congress asked for the project's state and for views on how FinCEN picks and steers tech buys. GAO laid out options the agency could weigh as it rethinks the build.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-987r:
A missing list of key defense buying posts is flagged in GAO letter GAO-06-987R, dated September 8, 2006. A 1990 law defines critical acquisition posts: senior roles with charge over costly defense buys. The Secretary of Defense must publish the list of such posts from time to time.

GAO learned of the gap while studying the space buying workforce. It asked if the department in fact publishes the list, as law requires. Work without that data, GAO warned, can flaw workforce choices and put missions at risk. The letter urges a directive to publish the data, plus steps to improve its quality and use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1037r:
Pay claims for people hurt by Cold War radiation are updated in GAO letter GAO-07-1037R, dated September 7, 2007. From 1945 through 1962 the United States ran open-air atomic tests. Uranium mining fed the same arsenal. Many workers and nearby people were exposed, and some fell ill.

A 1990 law set up pay for these victims, or their kin. The Justice Department runs the claims. A 2000 update widened who can claim, adding mill workers and ore haulers. Law tells GAO to report every 18 months. The letter gives the state of claims, and how the trust fund, set to end in 2022, stands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1157r:
Follow-up answers on a failed finance system make up GAO letter GAO-07-1157R, dated August 10, 2007. On June 28, 2007 GAO told a Senate panel of the Homeland Security Department's failed eMerge2 program. That program was meant to join finance systems across the whole department. It fell short.

A July 10, 2007 request asked for more answers. GAO based them on its past work for the hearing. The June testimony had set out the department's finance update efforts, its chief hurdles, and four building blocks for sound system work. The letter puts those added answers on the record, in the same frame.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1197r:
Guard rules for weapons-grade nuclear stock differ by agency, GAO reports in letter GAO-07-1197R, dated September 11, 2007. In set forms and sums, such stock is called Category I special nuclear material. In terror hands it could build a crude nuclear bomb. The Energy Department guards its own sites. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission licenses trade sites that hold such stock, mostly for the Energy Department.

Each side works from a secret design basis threat, a model of the attack to beat. Guards, fences, alarms, and a two-person rule back it up. Mock attack tests probe the guard. GAO set the two rule sets side by side, and noted the split.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-207r:
Freight rail rates fell for most shippers after deregulation, but grain shippers tell a different story. GAO summed up its rail findings in GAO-07-207R, a letter dated November 8, 2006. The letter presents highlights of GAO's October 2006 report on the industry. That report covered changes since the Staggers Rail Act of 1980. It also covered steps by the Surface Transportation Board on competition. Freight demand forecasts for the next 15 to 25 years were included.

From 1985 through 2004, rates generally decreased, GAO reported. But nominal grain rates rose 9 percent over that span. On some routes, more grain moved at rates well above the relief threshold. That threshold marks where the board may step in for captive shippers. The letter carries the findings in briefing slides. It points readers to the full October report for the analysis behind them.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-217r:
After a hearing on defense contracting, senators sent GAO written questions that needed written answers. GAO replied in GAO-07-217R, a letter dated December 21, 2006. The questions followed GAO's September 7, 2006 testimony to a Senate defense panel. That testimony covered habits that weaken the Pentagon's deals with contractors. The answers take up award fees, weapons program outcomes, and oversight of contractor work.

On fees, GAO explained how award and incentive fees form part of a contractor's profit. On weapons, it urged proof that technology works before full development starts. Programs that began with immature technology saw research costs grow 34.9 percent on average. Programs that began with mature technology grew only 4.8 percent. GAO also pressed for clear duties and real accountability. It said Congress should not bless programs that skip those steps.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-227r:
Steam tunnels under the Capitol carry heat and chilled water to 24 buildings. Workers said the tunnels were unsafe, and GAO checked in GAO-07-227R, a letter dated November 16, 2006. The Capitol Power Plant runs five walkable tunnels. In March 2006, tunnel workers wrote Congress about falling concrete, asbestos, and extreme heat. A workplace office had filed a complaint a month earlier. Some hazards had been flagged as early as 1999.

The cited hazards largely remain, GAO found. Crews had braced some weak concrete and required protective gear. A contractor judged three tunnels safe from collapse. Two more were still under review at the time. The architect's repair plan was incomplete, GAO said. It priced near-term repairs at about $119 million over 6 years. Longer-range work added $14.4 million. The plan skipped the options study the House had asked for.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-287r:
A senator asked one pointed question about claimed savings from a military travel system. GAO answered in GAO-07-287R, a letter dated December 19, 2006. The question followed GAO's November 16, 2006 testimony on the Defense Travel System. The program office had projected $56.4 million in personnel savings. Of that, $24.2 million was tied to the Army and Navy. The senator asked whether the savings assumed staff cuts. He also asked if gains in work speed could be measured instead.

The savings claims do not hold up, GAO replied. The Army and Navy have not cut staff through the system. Neither service expects to do so. GAO's September 2006 report had called the estimated $54.1 million in yearly personnel savings unrealistic. The assumptions behind the Navy and Air Force figures were not valid. The department offered no new data against that finding. GAO stood by its earlier conclusion.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-297r:
Old e-mails suggesting faked science at a nuclear waste project set off a costly response. GAO priced that response in GAO-07-297R, a letter dated January 19, 2007. The e-mails came from survey workers on the Yucca Mountain Project. They surfaced in March 2005. The Energy Department reviewed project mail and redid technical work. Water flow studies drew the most rework. The letter sends Congress slides from an October 23, 2006 briefing.

Reviews and probes cost about $4.2 million across fiscal years 2005 and 2006, GAO reports. Agency review work alone ran about $2.7 million. Three kinds of review combed a database of 14 million e-mails. They raised seven new issues. Outside reviews added about $530,000. Staff also got added management and quality training. The briefing priced finishing the whole project too. The department's schedule then aimed to open the site by 2017.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-317r:
Military families with special medical needs get steered to bases where care exists. GAO inventoried that care in GAO-07-317R, a letter dated March 16, 2007. Enrollment in the Exceptional Family Member Program is mandatory for such families. A 2005 law asked how the program affects nearby towns. GAO studied four communities with many enrolled families. It catalogued military and local services.

Military health care covers basics plus home care and respite care, GAO found. Family centers offer day care and activity programs. But some services are hard to reach. One naval hospital's lone child development specialist also serves other bases. A child with severe autism was turned away from a base program. Towns offer counseling and therapy as well. Yet no agency tracks how much enrolled families use local care. Specialist shortages strain military and civilian patients alike.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-327r: The Air Force Sergeants Association holds a federal charter, and GAO reviews its outside audits. GAO-07-327R, a letter dated January 26, 2007, reports that review for fiscal years 2006 and 2005. For both years, the auditor held that the group's statements were presented fairly under standard accounting rules. GAO's review found no breaches worth reporting.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-347r:
Radiation gates at ports cannot tell a bomb ingredient from harmless ceramic tile, and better models are costly. GAO found the test record scattered in GAO-07-347R, dated March 9, 2007. The nuclear detection office leads work on the gates. Older plastic gates sense radiation but cannot name it. Newer models promise to identify materials. GAO asked if the office had gathered past lab tests on the older gates. It also asked what states were told.

The office had not collected most lab test results, GAO found. It was only planning a full database. Without the data, it cannot fully weigh old gates against new ones. That gap matters before a multibillion-dollar switch. Field data on gate performance was also missing. Experts said the missing record could guide design and buying. States could use it for their own purchases. GAO urged collecting every lab report. The department generally concurred.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-367r:
The Air Force added passenger and cargo duties to its next tanker jet without the studies its own rules require. GAO reported the shortcut in GAO-07-367R, dated March 6, 2007. The current tanker fleet averages over 46 years of age. Replacement could cost $72 billion to $120 billion over decades. The service plans to cut 40,000 members in the same budget squeeze. GAO reviewed how the extra capability entered the plan.

No analysis showed a gap the extra capability must fill, GAO found. No analysis weighed the risk of leaving it out. Senior councils approved the requirement anyway. That approval came in November 2006. Without the missing studies, the program may fail certification. Certification is required before the purchase can begin. The gap could cost billions for an unneeded feature, GAO said. The defense department disagreed with GAO's advice to run the studies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-437r:
Child care and elder care needs among federal staff are measured in GAO-07-437R, a GAO letter report of March 30, 2007. Congress wanted to know how much care federal workers need. It also asked what share use federal help, such as child care centers and flexible schedules. The Office of Personnel Management ran a survey of staff, and GAO studied the results.

The letter reports how many workers said they need care for a child or an adult. It shows how they now meet those needs. It also tracks use of federal programs built for that purpose. The data matter because the workforce is split by age. Many staff near retirement care for aging parents. Younger hires more often need child care. The findings guide choices on work-life support.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-47r:
Older patients take more drugs yet join drug trials less, and GAO-07-47R, released September 28, 2007, studies the rules that shape that gap. People age 65 and older face more cancer, Parkinson's disease, and heart disorders. Age also slows the liver and kidneys, so side effects hit harder. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) says drugs should be tested in the old before approval.

GAO examined the guidance and rules FDA gives drug sponsors. One part covers how sponsors must report data on effects in older patients. The other covers how FDA medical officers weigh that data in drug reviews. Trial teams mix doctors, chemists, and statisticians. GAO's point is sharp: if few older patients join trials, no one can spot harms that show up only with age. The report maps where FDA's paper rules help and where they fall short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-667r:
Disabled veterans have a chartered advocate, and GAO-07-667R, dated April 5, 2007, reviews its audit. The Disabled American Veterans helps veterans and their families win the benefits and services they are owed. It also speaks for disabled veterans. Federal law requires the group, as a chartered corporation, to file full yearly statements and obtain an outside audit.

GAO's letter covers the fiscal year ended December 31, 2005. Staff read the audit report and the statements behind it and ran checks on the figures. They did not audit the group or give their own opinion. No reportable breach of the reporting rules was found. The auditors held the statements fairly presented under U.S. accounting standards. The letter joins a set of charter reviews GAO sent the same day.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-757r:
Legal advice inside the pension insurance agency is faulted in GAO-07-757R, a letter dated May 18, 2007. The Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation insures pensions for nearly 44 million workers. In fiscal year 2006, it paid $4.1 billion to about 612,000 people. In 2005, it split its legal work between two offices. A new chief counsel's office took core mission issues. The general counsel kept general law topics. GAO checked whether the split served the agency well.

Staff faced confusion over which office owned each question. Advice could differ between the two shops. GAO urged one chief legal officer over all legal work. That step would give the director one clear source of counsel. Four past general counsels backed the same view in talks with GAO. Without a single chief, GAO warned, mixed advice will persist. The agency's legal load grows as more weak pension plans fail.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-767r:
Defense Department reports on improper payments are reviewed in GAO-07-767R, a letter dated May 31, 2007. The Improper Payments Information Act of 2002 forces agencies to hunt for payments made in error. They must estimate the sums and report steps to cut them. The department has reported such data since 2003. Its reports now cover six programs, from military pay to health benefits. Congress told GAO to focus on travel pay.

The department's inspector general found major flaws in its fiscal year 2006 effort. In fiscal year 2005, the department said no program met the risk bar for reporting. Its own survey still flagged military pay as a risk. Past GAO work found waste in travel claims, first-class flights, and unused tickets. This letter tracks how travel pay figures entered the department's public reports. It tests whether the reporting meets the law's demands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-787r:
Care for troops hurt by vaccines is covered in GAO-07-787R, a letter GAO sent on June 29, 2007. Over 2.2 million service members get at least one required shot each year. Most side effects are mild, such as swelling. A few troops had severe reactions to the anthrax and smallpox vaccines. In September 2001, the Defense Department set up the Vaccine Healthcare Centers Network. GAO reviewed what the network does and how well it is known.

The network treats patients, studies safer vaccine use, and teaches staff and troops. It can guide care from afar when a patient sits far from a center. Officials praised its clinical care in talks with GAO. Its teaching may not reach enough providers, though. Many health staff do not know the network's role. A December 2006 move put the network under the military vaccine agency. That step gives it a formal home and mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1007r:
Hunger in sub-Saharan Africa is the subject of GAO report GAO-08-1007R of July 17, 2008. At the 1996 World Food Summit, world leaders pledged to halve the number of undernourished people by 2015. That pledge was renewed in the Millennium Development Goals in 2000. Yet about 850 million people, including 170 million children, remain undernourished.

In sub-Saharan Africa, the count rose from about 170 million in 1990 to 1992 to over 200 million in 2001 to 2003. Food riots have broken out in 15 countries since early 2007, seven of them in that region. GAO traces why numbers have not fallen and what efforts are under way. The report shows how far the 2015 goal stands from reach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-137r:
AIDS funding shifts for cities are modeled in GAO letter GAO-08-137R, dated October 5, 2007. The Ryan White CARE Act of 1990 funds care for people with HIV and AIDS. A December 2006 law renewed the programs through fiscal year 2009. A House bill for fiscal year 2008 would shield city areas from funding losses.

City grants flow through three streams: formula awards, need-based awards, and a minority initiative. GAO weighed how the House shield would change what urban areas receive. The Senate had not passed the bill at the time. The letter gives lawmakers a clear view of who gains and who loses under the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-257r:
Rebuilding the Army's floating stockpiles is faulted in GAO letter GAO-08-257R, dated February 8, 2008. The Army stores unit equipment sets on ships and at sites worldwide. Troops can then deploy in days rather than weeks. Wars in Iraq and Afghanistan have drained much of that stock. Prior GAO testimony in 2006 and 2007 flagged the toll on gear.

This letter finds the refill effort half-planned. The Army has not fully planned the rebuild of its afloat stocks. It has not fully budgeted for it either. Repair and replacement face long delays and rising costs. The letter shows a readiness debt still waiting for a payment plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-267r:
A running count of Haitian immigration cases fills GAO letter GAO-08-267R of November 16, 2007. A 1998 law let certain Haitian nationals and their families seek permanent residence. The law orders the Comptroller General to report every 6 months until all cases close. This letter is the seventeenth such report.

Through September 30, 2007, the immigration service had received 41,370 applications. It had approved 18,886 of them. Immigration courts held 2,098 more filings and had approved 827. The letter sorts applicants by class, from asylum seekers and parolees to orphaned children. It adds the tallies for spouses and other dependents.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-297r:
Lawmakers' questions on the digital television aid plan are answered in GAO letter GAO-08-297R of November 19, 2007. Members wrote to GAO on November 7, 2007, after a hearing on the switch to digital broadcasts. They asked whether GAO holds concerns about the converter box subsidy. That program helps antenna households buy boxes before analog signals end.

The letter also answers a funding question. Should the telecom agency brace for a shortfall in the subsidy pot, and plan how to handle one? A third answer explains the legal basis for a joint task force on the switch. GAO grounds its replies in work done that November.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-307r:
Water project cost shares in California are detailed in GAO letter GAO-08-307R of December 18, 2007. The Central Valley Project is a web of dams, canals, and pumps built from 1960 onward. Its San Luis Unit, south of the delta, was raised jointly by federal and state builders. Four irrigation districts draw its water. Westlands alone covers about three-quarters of the unit's land.

Each district holds a federal water contract at a set rate per acre-foot. Contracts can be renewed for up to 25 years. The letter works through how the districts repay the capital building costs of the unit. It lays out the shares behind a long-running water bargain.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-347r:
High-voltage direct-current transmission lines along transport routes are covered in GAO letter report GAO-08-347R, dated February 1, 2008. The nation has more than 150,000 miles of high-voltage lines, and rising demand has strained the grid. Some firms propose new direct-current lines that would follow active transportation rights of way.

States have long made most siting calls, with the federal role largely limited to federal land. The Energy Policy Act of 2005 widened that role: the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission may now permit lines in designated national interest corridors. Federal and state guidance already favors placing new lines along existing rights of way. Stakeholders worried the wider federal role could crowd out state review and public input; the commission said it would weigh state records and public comment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-377r:
Federal improper payment estimates for fiscal year 2007 are summed up in GAO letter GAO-08-377R, dated January 23, 2008. Under the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002, major agencies must estimate payments made in error. Congress asked GAO for summary data and early analysis of the new figures.

Agencies reported about $55 billion in improper payments for fiscal year 2007, up from $41 billion the year before. Most of the rise came from one part of Medicaid reporting improper payments for the first time, at about $13 billion. GAO called the wider reporting a good step toward showing the full scale of the problem. The letter draws on agencies' performance and accountability reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-387r:
A Defense Department pilot for handling equal employment opportunity complaints is reviewed in GAO letter GAO-08-387R, dated February 22, 2008. Three components — the Air Force, the Defense Logistics Agency, and the Defense Commissary Agency — tested new complaint processes from 2004. GAO had warned in May 2006 that the pilot's evaluation plan was weak.

Two pilots leaned on alternative dispute resolution at the informal stage, while the Air Force merged the inquiry and hearing stages to cut processing time. Take-up varied widely: under 20 percent of those offered the Air Force pilot joined, while over 95 percent accepted the Defense Logistics Agency pilot. The department fixed parts of its evaluation plan, so the Air Force pilot can now be judged soundly. The other two pilots still cannot yield valid results, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-397r:
Posthearing answers on servicemembers' job rights are given in GAO letter GAO-08-397R, dated January 10, 2008. The letter follows GAO's November 8, 2007 testimony to a Senate committee on the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act. Senators' questions focus on how federal agencies handle USERRA claims.

GAO explained that some claims take far longer than agency data suggest. Of 10,061 formal complaints filed with the Department of Labor from October 1, 1996, through June 30, 2005, more than 430 were closed and reopened at least once. For 52 cases closed and reopened two or more times, the true wait averaged about 20 to 21 months. The gaps between closure and reopening were not captured in Labor's database. The answers also cover the federal-sector demonstration project for such complaints.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-537r:
Cost estimates for World Trade Center health programs are checked in GAO letter GAO-08-537R, dated March 11, 2008. Federal funds for screening, monitoring, and treating attack responders totaled $261.1 million from October 2001 through November 2007. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health runs the grant programs.

GAO had found the fiscal year 2007 estimate unreliable, since it rested on shaky assumptions and proxy payment data. The fiscal year 2008 process improved, GAO reports. The institute used real average costs from the April through June 2007 quarter for exams and for outpatient care, which made up almost two-thirds of the estimate. Counts of responders to screen also rested on real program data this time. Health officials agreed the new process is better.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-557r:
War spending obligations are tallied in GAO letter GAO-08-557R, dated March 17, 2008. Congress has given the Defense Department hundreds of billions since 2001 for the Global War on Terrorism. Reported yearly obligations grew from about $0.2 billion in fiscal year 2001 to about $139.8 billion in fiscal year 2007.

For fiscal year 2008, the President sought $189.3 billion. Through December 2007, Congress had provided about $86.8 billion of it, including $16.8 billion for mine resistant vehicles. The remaining $102.5 billion awaited action as of February 2008. The letter breaks reported obligations through December 2007 down by service and account. Future costs, GAO notes, hinge on the pace of operations, troop facilities, redeployment, and gear repair.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-577r:
Millennium Challenge Corporation compacts are analyzed in GAO letter GAO-08-577R, dated April 11, 2008. The corporation aids countries that rule justly, free their economies, and invest in their people. It has received over $7.5 billion for fiscal years 2004 to 2008 and set aside about $6.4 billion for compact aid.

By March 2008, 28 countries were eligible and 16 had signed compacts. Deals now take far longer to build: the first 11 averaged 25 months from selection to signing, and the average for all 16 is headed to 32 months. At that pace, GAO projects the corporation can commit its current funds by the end of 2009. Spending lags plans in all 11 countries with compacts in force.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-827r:
Private Medicare plans must tell the government how they expect to split each dollar between care, overhead, and profit. Payments rest in part on those forecasts. GAO-08-827R, a letter dated June 24, 2008, compares real 2005 results with the forecasts for 120 contracts.

Plans spent 85.7 percent of revenue on care, not the 90.2 percent they had forecast. Profits came in at 5.1 percent of revenue, about $1.14 billion above forecast. A few outlier contracts drove more than half that gap. Nearly two-thirds of members sat in plans where the profit share beat the forecast by a wide margin in that year.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-927r:
A single personnel and pay system for all services is the subject of GAO-08-927R, a September 2008 letter to the Secretary of Defense. The Defense Integrated Military Human Resources System, begun in February 1998, aims to replace the patchwork of service-run pay systems. Those systems produced late and wrong pay, seen in the early 1990s, when Army Reserve and National Guard troops got late or wrong pay after the Desert Shield and Desert Storm operations. The Army is the first service set to deploy it.

The letter's title carries the finding: keeping communication effective is needed to help the Army's rollout succeed. Development has been under way since DOD accepted the first-phase design in November 2004. How well the program talks with the Army and its users, the letter argues, can decide whether a long-troubled modernization finally lands.
